name: Flensburg
title: Thickness Measurement in Flensburg | Coasters & Ro-Ro Ships
description: Thickness measurement in Flensburg for coasters, bulk and general cargo ships and ro-ro tonnage: hold, hatch cover, ballast tank and piping gauging alongside.
h1: Ship Thickness Gauging on the Flensburg Fjord: Coasters, Cargo Ships and Ro-Ro Tonnage
intro: Flensburg lies at the head of a long, sheltered fjord on the Danish border, with a commercial harbour serving coasters in the grain, feed, fertiliser and building-materials trades, and a shipyard known for its ro-ro newbuildings. Ships here are small and their calls are short, so a cargo stop is usually the only chance to gauge holds, hatch covers and tanks between dockings. Atlantis sends its technicians from India for every job, timed to the ship's berth slot rather than to a fixed schedule.

highlights.p: Grain, animal feed and fertiliser move through Flensburg on small dry-cargo ships. Fertiliser in particular eats into hold steel, and the time between discharge and the next loading is when hold frames, tank tops and lower brackets can be measured.

highlights.h: Hatch covers that see every cargo
highlights.p: On ships calling at short intervals, hatch covers are opened and closed many times a week. Panel plating, coaming tops and compression bars wear and corrode, and gauging them during a harbour stop helps keep the holds weathertight.

highlights.h: Steel traditional ships in the fjord
highlights.p: Flensburg's historic harbour is home to traditional ships, some of them steel-hulled. Their owners use thickness readings to plan plating repairs before a slipping, and winter, when the ships are laid up, gives the longest access.

port.h: Flensburg: a border fjord with a working harbour
p: The Flensburg Fjord runs inland from the western Baltic between the German shore of Angeln and the Danish shore of Sønderjylland, narrowing as it goes until it ends at the city. The border follows the water for much of the way, so a ship bound for Flensburg passes Danish coastline to starboard and German coastline to port. The water is sheltered, tidal range in the Baltic is small, and there are no locks or bridges to pass, which makes the fjord easy to reach for coasters and short-sea traders. Its length, though, means a call at Flensburg is a deliberate destination rather than a stop on the way somewhere else, and ships come in for a cargo, a lay-by or a yard appointment, then head back out the way they came. In strong easterly weather the outer fjord can be lively, while the inner harbour stays calm.

Commercial traffic is modest and regional. Small dry-cargo ships bring in feed, fertiliser and building materials and take out grain from the farms of northern Schleswig-Holstein, working the quays of the inner harbour. The Flensburger Schiffbau-Gesellschaft (FSG) on the eastern shore has built ro-ro and ro-pax ships for European and overseas operators for decades, and after an insolvency the yard changed owner in 2025. Passenger traffic is mostly excursion boats working the fjord in the summer months. The city's long maritime history shows in its historic harbour, where traditional ships and museum vessels lie alongside, and several of the traditional ships based here still take guests to sea each season. Workboats, tugs and small service craft based in the harbour complete the picture.

For gauging, the rhythm is set by the cargo. A coaster may be alongside for a day or less, discharging with grabs or by conveyor and then loading the next cargo for another Baltic or North Sea port. The interval between cargoes, when holds are empty and swept, is the useful window, and the crew's preparation determines how much of it goes on measurement. Superintendents of these ships are often managing several small vessels at once, sometimes from Germany, the Netherlands or Denmark, and value a defined scope finished inside a single call. Winter brings fewer cargo calls but more idle ships, including traditional vessels in lay-up. Harvest season works the other way: when grain starts moving in late summer, berths fill and turnarounds shorten, so a superintendent who wants a hold gauged then should tell us early.

facilities.h: Where gauging happens on the Flensburg waterfront
p: The quays of the commercial harbour are where most cargo-ship gauging takes place. The ship lies alongside, holds and ballast tanks can be opened in turn, and road access to the quay makes it straightforward to bring equipment aboard. FSG is a newbuilding yard rather than a repair dock, and Flensburg has no commercial drydock taking outside work, so ships due for a docking survey go to repair yards on the Danish islands, in Kiel or further afield. Readings taken in Flensburg before that docking give the yard and the class surveyor a head start on the steel list.

Lay-by berths in the inner harbour are used by ships waiting for cargo and by vessels out of service, and those are the best places for longer programmes such as pre-purchase or reactivation gauging. Traditional ships are usually examined at their own berths in the historic harbour during winter lay-up, when tanks and bilges can be cleaned and opened without pressure from a sailing season. Ships anchored in the outer fjord can be reached by boat for small scopes, though most owners prefer to keep the work for a berth.
list: Commercial harbour quays — hold, hatch cover, double-bottom and ballast tank gauging on coasters between discharge and loading.
Inner harbour lay-by berths — pre-purchase, on-hire and reactivation gauging on cargo ships waiting for work or out of service.
Historic harbour berths — hull plating and frame gauging on steel traditional ships during winter lay-up.
Outer fjord anchorage — small, pre-planned scopes by boat when a ship is waiting for its berth and conditions allow.
Docking yards in Denmark, Kiel and beyond — Flensburg readings passed to the yard and class surveyor ahead of steel renewal.

context.h: Small ships, border waters and EU reporting rules
p: A ship alongside in Flensburg is subject to German port state control under the Paris MoU, carried out by the Ship Safety Division of BG Verkehr; the Danish shore of the fjord falls to the Danish Maritime Authority, which matters only for ships calling on that side. The small dry-cargo ships that use the harbour are often older, frequently flagged in Europe's open registers, and inspected regularly because of their age. Hold structure, hatch covers and air pipes are common subjects of deficiencies on such ships, and a superintendent who knows their condition can answer an inspector's questions with evidence rather than assurances.

Most coasters calling here fall below the 5,000 GT line that brings ships into the EU Emissions Trading System, but EU rules still reach them. General cargo ships from 400 GT upward have had to monitor and report their emissions under the EU MRV regulation since 2025, and ships of any flag calling at EU ports need an Inventory of Hazardous Materials. Owners weighing whether an ageing coaster is worth another five-year cycle therefore want the hull and hold condition quantified before they commit to a renewal survey and its steel.

jobs.p: Flensburg work is mostly short, focused gauging on small cargo ships, scoped by a superintendent who already knows which part of the ship is the concern, often from the last class report or a port state inspection. Holds and hatch covers come first on ships in the fertiliser and feed trades, ballast tanks on ships approaching an intermediate or renewal survey. The crew's part is to have holds swept, tanks emptied and ventilated, and permits ready before the team boards. Occasional longer jobs come from sales, from ships returning to service, and from traditional ships preparing for a slipping. Examples:
list: A coaster after discharging fertiliser: hold frames, lower brackets and tank-top plating gauged before the hold is washed and reloaded with grain.
A general cargo ship awaiting its next fixture at a lay-by berth: hatch cover panels, coamings and compression-bar seats measured and checked for cracks.
Pre-purchase gauging of a small bulk carrier for a Scandinavian buyer: holds, ballast tanks and deck plating measured in a single stay alongside.
A steel traditional ship in winter lay-up: hull plating and frames gauged from inside the hull to plan plate renewals before the next slipping.
A short-sea ship ahead of an intermediate survey: selected ballast tanks gauged in Flensburg so the steel estimate is ready for the docking yard.

logistics: The team usually lands at Hamburg Airport and continues by rail through Neumünster to Flensburg, on a direct regional line; Billund in Denmark is an alternative for some itineraries. Germany and Denmark are both Schengen states, so a single Schengen visa covers jobs on either side of the fjord. The ship's agent books the berth window, arranges harbour access and confirms gas-free and entry arrangements with the master, and we tie the flights to that window.
vessels: Coasters and short-sea general cargo ships

faqs.q: Can holds be gauged on a coaster between two cargoes at Flensburg?
faqs.a: Yes, if the hold can be swept and lit and the crew can rig safe access to frames and tank top. The window between discharge and loading is often only hours, so we agree beforehand which hold comes first and which frames and brackets matter most. After a fertiliser or feed cargo, residues are removed before readings are taken, because they hide the surface and attack the steel.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock in Flensburg for repairs?
faqs.a: Flensburg's shipyard builds new ro-ro ships rather than taking outside repairs, and the harbour has no commercial drydock for visiting cargo ships. Ships needing a docking usually go to repair yards in Denmark, Kiel or further afield. Gauging in Flensburg is done afloat, and the readings can be handed to the docking yard so steel renewal is priced and planned in advance.

faqs.q: Do you gauge traditional and sail-training ships?
faqs.a: Steel-hulled traditional ships can be gauged like any other steel hull, from inside where frames and plating can be reached. Winter lay-up is the best time, because ballast, bilges and tanks can be cleared without interrupting a sailing season. The owner and the surveyor decide which areas need readings; we provide the measurements and a sketch-based report that a yard can work from.

faqs.q: What happens if a ship has to wait at anchor in the fjord?
faqs.a: A small scope can be done at anchor by boat, provided the agent can arrange the boat and boarding is safe. In practice, most owners keep hold and tank work for the berth, where the ship is steady, power is available and the crew can open spaces more easily. Waiting time at anchor is better used by the crew to prepare tanks for the team's arrival.
